Abraham Lincoln. On November 19, 1863, four months after the Battle of Gettysburg, he spoke at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery in Pennsylvania. His remarks were brief—only two hundred and seventy-two words—yet they became one of history's most consequential political statements.

Lincoln opened with a famous line: "Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal." He redefned the war's purpose. This was not merely a struggle to preserve the Union, but a struggle for a new birth of freedom—a moral reckoning with slavery itself. The nation would be reborn through sacrifice, employing birth and renewal as his central metaphors.

Lincoln's actual delivery was brief, and the main oration by Edward Everett, which lasted two hours, was forgotten. Yet Lincoln's address endured as the canonical statement. The phrase "the last full measure of devotion," describing the soldiers' sacrifice, became shorthand for ultimate civic commitment. Delivered amid ongoing tragedy, the speech resolved the catastrophe into moral purpose, reshaping American identity through the vision of democratic renewal.
